title: How do you organize your development?
author: Ok-Philosopher333
selftext:
How do you organize building your game system by system in a way that you will have building blocks to plug in later so you don’t have to worry about breaking functional systems, while also ensuring they will actually work together?

My failure: Unreal Engine: Built a working stealth system and enemy ai that could search and chase player, etc. using AI to teach and build nodes step by step. Eventually although the system worked it built itself off maintaining a constant web of interconnected logic that sprawled and eventually I called it quits knowing it would derail future developments.

comments.author: Skubcraft
comments.body:
Regression testing systems that runs tests for every change made.  That way if something breaks you'll know right away.  

Talk to your agent about this and it can give you more info about building this up.

comments.author: Alarmed_Outcome3749
comments.body:
How I organize it, building games with Claude uses a standard reusable kit for each game all stored in GitHub and backed up in Google drive automatically with each release. 

One rulebook. All my games share a numbered standards file. The AI reads it at the start of every session, so every system follows the same patterns.

A shared kit. Settings, saves, controller input and menus live in one repo. Each game pulls a fixed version. Fix a bug once and every game gets the fix.

Systems never reach into each other. They talk through events. Stealth announces "player spotted." Enemy AI listens and reacts. Neither one knows how the other works inside. In Unreal, Event Dispatchers or Blueprint Interfaces do this job.

One area first. Get one small slice fully working before adding more.

Small releases. Each release tests only what changed.
A debug menu. Jump to any area or turn any feature on or off to test one system alone.

Handoff notes. Each session ends with a handoff file, so the next one starts with full context.

The sprawl you hit usually comes from the AI wiring systems straight into each other. Give it the rules before it builds anything and hold it to them.

replies.author: PoopsMcScoots
replies.body:
Damn, that’s really smart,

Keep chats short and quarantine everything.

replies.author: Ok-Philosopher333
replies.body: At what stages do you decide to upload?

replies.author: StellarSoupStudio
replies.body: I'm using Vercel preview branches and I have access to Claude Code Projects which is an orchestration layer. So when I have claude add a new feature it makes it on a new branch, opens a PR, and I can preview it in the PR branch on Vercel. If it works the way I want then I merge the branch into main, if it's not there yet I go back to the chat window and paste in logs & feedback.

replies.author: Redshirt_Down
replies.body: Immediately. Ask Claude to build a git and testing framework and then have it dispatch agents to run them.

comments.author: Sacred_B
comments.body: I have only done two big projects so far, but both times working up a design document with an agent really helps. Sometimes I think of something because of a choice the agent presents, or sometimes it catches dependency issues before code is even written. Let it plan what it's going to do for the most part.
